## Two jobs, one curve

::: {.none}
**Description** – map how the estimate moves across every defensible choice. *(What we have been doing all day.)*

::: {.fragment}
**Inference** – ask whether the curve *as a whole* is surprising if there were no effect at all. *(A different, harder job.)*
:::

::: {.fragment}
The two are detachable, and most published curves stop at description.
:::
:::

::: {.src}
[@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse; @SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis]
:::

::: notes
Last conceptual move of the day, and it is the one that separates careful readers of specification curves from impressed ones. A curve like ours does two different jobs. The first is description: showing how the estimate moves as the choices move – that is what we built, and it is genuinely valuable on its own. The second is inference: asking whether the curve, taken as a whole, is more extreme than you would expect if there were no effect at all. Those are different questions with different machinery, and they detach cleanly – Multi100 did the description without the inference, and so, so far, have we. The next three slides are about what the second job takes.
:::

## 840 estimates are not 840 tests

::: {.small}
- Every specification re-uses the **same 270 country-years** – the estimates are deeply dependent
- '63.9% significant' **describes** the curve; it is not a p-value for the claim
- Vote-counting across dependent specifications has no null distribution – you cannot just tally the stars
:::

::: notes
Here is the trap the percentages set. Sixty-three point nine per cent of our specifications are significant. It is very tempting to read that as evidence strength: "most tests pass, so the claim holds". But all eight hundred and forty specifications interrogate the same two hundred and seventy country-years. They share the data, so they share the noise: if sampling luck pushed a handful of country-years the claim's way, it pushed hundreds of specifications the same way at once. The percentage significant is a description of the curve, not a test of the claim. To test the claim at curve level you need to know what the whole curve would look like if there were nothing to find – and that requires building the nothing.
:::

## Building the nothing: the permutation design

::: {.small}
- Break the one link the claim needs: **shuffle each country's unemployment series in time** (jointly with growth), keeping everything else intact
- Refit **all 840 specifications** on each shuffled dataset · repeat **B = 500** times
- Compare the observed curve to the 500 null curves: is ours more extreme than chance produces?
:::

::: {.src}
The design is worked through in your inference reading; permutation inference after [@PhipsonSmyth2010PermutationPValues].
:::

::: notes
The nothing is built like this. The claim says a country's unemployment moves its EU framing over time. So take each country and shuffle its unemployment series in time – together with growth, so the macro side stays internally coherent – while leaving the framing data untouched. In a shuffled world the alignment between unemployment and framing is broken by construction: whatever curve you get is what pure chance produces on these exact data with these exact 840 specifications. Do that five hundred times, refit the entire grid each time, and you have five hundred ghost curves to stand ours against. If our curve sits in the far tail of those ghosts, the curve as a whole is evidence. If it sits comfortably among them – the description stands, but the inference does not.
:::

## How to read a curve-level test {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- With B = 500, the smallest reportable p is **2/(B+1) ≈ 0.004** – a floor, not a zero
- Near p = .05 the Monte-Carlo wobble is about **±0.01**, so treat p = .04 and p = .06 as the same finding
- [A DESIGN · NOT YET RUN]{.highlight bg-colour="#ffe3b3"} – a curve-level test has to be fixed in advance, and this one has not been run; today we read the design, not a result
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Discussion (2 minutes, then chat):** the constrained cosmopolitan-only universe has 140 specs: **70.7% negative, 57.1% negative *and* significant.** Strong evidence? *Against what null?*
:::

::: notes
Two literacy points and then you argue. First: with five hundred draws, the smallest p-value the test can report is two over five hundred and one – about point zero zero four. That is a resolution floor, not a zero; more draws buy sharper floors at real compute cost. Second: near the point-oh-five boundary the Monte-Carlo wobble is around plus or minus point zero one, so a permutation p of point zero four and point zero six are the same finding twice. And the badge matters: this test is designed, not run – you are reading a plan today, which is itself the preregistration lesson again. Now the discussion beat. The constrained universe – cosmopolitan outcome only, 140 specifications – is 70.7 per cent negative, 57.1 per cent negative and significant. Two minutes: is that strong evidence? Against what null? Type your answer. [harvest: the sharp ones will say – we don't know until we know what chance produces on these dependent data; that is exactly the point.]
:::

## What stands without the test

::: {.small}
- Everything descriptive survives: the **49.7%** outcome fork · the analysts' placement · the sign-flip anatomy · the correction arc · **your dot**
- What waits for the permutation: the sentence "the curve as a whole is unlikely under no effect"
- Careful reporting says which of the two layers a claim lives in
:::

::: notes
So that nothing feels deflated: notice how much of today needs no permutation at all. That the outcome fork carries half the variance – description, stands. That the two person-level analysts bracket the range – stands. That the sign flips concentrate in the pooled estimator and the non-bailout samples – stands. The correction arc, your preregistered dot, the whole anatomy of the curve – all of it stands. The single sentence that has to wait is "this curve as a whole is unlikely if there is no effect". Keeping those two layers apart in your own writing – saying which one your claim lives in – puts you ahead of most published specification curves. That is inference literacy, and you now have it.
:::

## The multiverse has its critics {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- "Robustness is better assessed with a **few thoughtful models** than with billions of regressions" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed; answering @GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources] – only *justified* models targeting the *same estimand* belong in one curve. Today's grid is a **curated 840**, not billions, and the fork chart does the job every critic endorses: it locates where the argument must happen
- "**There is only one correct analysis**" once the question is fully specified [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne] – your declared specification answers *cherry-picking*, and their deeper point is that declaring in advance does not yet make a choice *justified*, which is what the estimand and DAG work were for
- "What's a multiverse **good for** anyway?" – reflection, persuasion, or inference, and each purpose wants a *differently built* universe [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood]. Today's was built for **reflection**, and how much more to read into it is the open debate
:::

::: {.src}
The book-length how-to: [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational]; the estimand diagnosis behind Block 2: [@AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial].
:::

::: notes
One last literacy layer: the method you practised is under live debate, and you can now read it. Katrin Auspurg – Block 2's estimand diagnosis – answered a 3.6-billion-estimate study with the line at the top of this slide: only thoughtful, justified models belong in a curve. Today mostly agreed with her: our grid is a curated eight hundred and forty, not an enumeration, and the fork chart does the one job every critic endorses – it tells you where the argument has to happen. Lakens and colleagues say that once the question is fixed, only one analysis implements it correctly. Your preregistration answered cherry-picking; their deeper point – that declaring early does not make a choice justified – is exactly why we built the DAG before declaring. And Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman ask what a multiverse is for: reflection, persuasion, or inference – each wanting a differently built set. Ours was built for reflection. How much more to read into it is the debate you have now joined. [advance]
:::

## Two sentences worth keeping

::: {.claimcard}
"the common single-path analyses in social and behavioural research should not be simply assumed to be robust to alternative analyses" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]
:::

::: {.claimcard}
A blueprint: precise question → causal reasoning (DAG) → multiverse → sensitivity analysis [@AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial]
:::

::: {.small}
- Same-conclusion robustness and same-*number* robustness are different bars
- Justifiability is the criterion – choose with reasons, show the spread
:::

::: notes
Two sentences to take away. From the Multi100 paper: single-path analyses should not simply be assumed robust. And notice what preregistration did and did not do for you today – it protected your choice from being opportunistic, but it gave your declared dot no special status inside the curve. You lived both halves: the declaration made your one path defensible, and the grid showed it was still just one path among 840. That pairing – declare your path, then show the space it sits in – is the whole method. From Auspurg and Brüderl, the constructive recipe we followed: precise question, explicit assumptions, multiverse, sensitivity. And keep the two robustness standards apart in your own writing: same *conclusion* – seventy-four per cent in Multi100 – and same *number* – thirty-four. When you claim robustness, say which one you mean.
:::

## Git: the tool we left out

::: {.small}
- Today ran with **no version control at all**. That is a deliberate design, so nothing stood between you and the analysis
- What a git history would add: a **timestamped public trail** of every change – the workshop's first cohort even preregistered by commit message, letting git supply the timestamp
- The **companion module** on the site takes you from a plain folder to a published repository, at your own pace – your workspace zip is the perfect practice project
:::

::: notes
One tool we deliberately left out of today, named on the way out. Everything you did ran without version control – that was a design decision, not an oversight, because the first delivery taught me that git alongside everything else is one skill too many for a single day. But the skill is worth having: a git history is a timestamped public trail of every change you ever made, so every correction you ever apply sits in plain sight with a date on it. The first cohort of this workshop actually preregistered with a commit message, letting git supply the timestamp we got today from a rendered report. The site has a self-study companion module that takes you from a plain folder – your workspace zip is ideal – to a published repository. At your own pace, with nothing riding on it. That is the last tool in the kit.
:::
